title: Ivy League + MIT/Stanford/Caltech — STEM admit benchmarks
scope: The 8 Ivy League schools plus MIT, Stanford, and Caltech (11 schools). Figures are STEM-relevant admit benchmarks drawn from each school's most recent available Common Data Set (CDS) and official admissions pages, supplemented by reputable aggregators where the official PDF was not directly machine-readable.
caveats: SAT/ACT 25th/75th percentile ranges from test-optional cycles (Brown, Columbia, Cornell, Dartmouth Class of 2028, Stanford Class of 2028, etc.) are upward-biased because only stronger testers chose to submit. Several schools (MIT, Caltech, Harvard, Yale, Penn, Dartmouth, Brown, Stanford-from-2030) have since reinstated testing.
Most Ivy/peer CDS reports publish only 25th and 75th composite percentiles, so p50 is frequently null rather than fabricated.
These schools report class-rank bands (CDS C11) rather than a mean GPA; GPA notes reflect that.
EC/spike patterns are factual synthesis from official 'what we look for' pages and admissions guidance, not per-applicant statistics.

schools.name: Massachusetts Institute of Technology

gpa.note: MIT reports no mean GPA; ~92% of admitted students ranked in the top 5% of their high school class. SAT Math mid-50% is roughly 780-800.

ecPatterns: National/international olympiad distinction (USAMO, USAPhO, USACO, USNCO; Olympiad team members heavily overrepresented)
Original research with concrete output (ISEF/Regeneron STS finalists)
Maker/builder spikes — shipped software, built hardware, robotics
Deep single-domain STEM 'spike' over broad resume padding

insights: Across all 11 schools the STEM admit bar clusters tightly: composite SAT mid-50% roughly 1500-1580 and ACT 33-36. A score below ~1500 SAT / 33 ACT is a meaningful outlier at every school here.
The math half of the SAT effectively must be near-perfect for STEM admits — MIT's SAT Math mid-50% runs ~780-800. For STEM applicants the EBRW score has more slack than the math score.

Testing has swung back to required: MIT, Caltech, Harvard, Yale (test-flexible), Penn, Dartmouth, Brown require scores, and Stanford requires them starting the Class of 2030. Of this set only Columbia, Cornell, and Princeton were still test-optional in their most recent published cycle — so a strong score is increasingly non-negotiable.

Grades/rank are necessary but not differentiating: 90%+ of admits sit in the top 10% (often top 5%) of their high school class. Above that floor, the decision is driven by the 'spike,' not by squeezing out the last tenth of GPA.

The consistent STEM differentiator is concrete, externally-validated output: olympiad placement (USAMO/USAPhO/USACO Platinum/USNCO), science-fair recognition (ISEF, Regeneron STS), or published/mentored research — not club titles. Caltech states this most explicitly ('depth' over breadth; what you produced, not your position).

Computer Science is the #1 or #2 most-conferred major at essentially all 11 schools, so the CS applicant pool is the most saturated — a USACO Platinum/Gold record or shipped software project is closer to table stakes than a bonus for CS-track applicants.

Per-college fit matters at the school level: Cornell, Penn, and Princeton admit into specific colleges/schools (Engineering, Wharton, SEAS), so a STEM spike should be aimed at the right division, while Brown rewards a spike that bridges STEM with another field via the Open Curriculum.
